m-iliopsoas.summary: The strongest flexor of the hip, running from the posterior abdominal wall to the thigh. It is formed by psoas major and iliacus joining in a common tendon.
facts: Psoas major: vertebral bodies and discs of T12–L4 and transverse processes of L1–L5; iliacus: iliac fossa
Lesser trochanter of the femur
Psoas major: anterior rami of L1–L3; iliacus: femoral nerve (L2–L3)
Iliolumbar artery, lumbar arteries, deep circumflex iliac artery
Flexes the hip (climbing stairs, lifting the foot); with the thigh fixed it flexes the trunk (sitting up from lying)
sections: The branches of the lumbar plexus form within psoas; the femoral nerve emerges in the groove between psoas and iliacus, the obturator nerve from the medial border of psoas. Abscesses can track down the psoas sheath to the groin.
clinical: A psoas abscess (especially in tuberculous spondylitis) tracks down to the groin and thigh.
Psoas sign in appendicitis: passive extension of the right hip causes pain.
tus: Psoas major is supplied by lumbar plexus branches, iliacus by the femoral nerve.
A tuberculous psoas abscess can track along the muscle sheath to the groin and thigh.

m-gluteus-maximus.summary: The largest and heaviest muscle in the body, giving the buttock its rounded shape. In humans it is specialised for upright posture and walking.
facts: Outer surface of the ilium (behind the posterior gluteal line), back of the sacrum and coccyx, sacrotuberous ligament, thoracolumbar fascia
Iliotibial tract (most fibres) and gluteal tuberosity of the femur
Inferior gluteal nerve (L5–S2)
Superior and inferior gluteal arteries
Extends and externally rotates the hip; acts powerfully when rising from sitting, climbing stairs and running; stabilises the knee through the iliotibial tract
clinical: Intramuscular injections into the buttock are given in the upper outer quadrant (or ventrogluteal site) to avoid the sciatic nerve.
When the muscle is weak the trunk is thrown backwards when walking (gluteus maximus gait).
tus: Most of gluteus maximus inserts into the iliotibial tract, its deep fibres into the gluteal tuberosity.

m-gluteus-medius.summary: A fan-shaped muscle beneath gluteus maximus on the outer surface of the ilium. It keeps the pelvis level when walking.
facts: Outer surface of the ilium (between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines)
Lateral surface of the greater trochanter
Superior gluteal nerve (L4–S1)
Superior gluteal artery
Abducts and internally rotates the hip; prevents the opposite side of the pelvis dropping when standing on one leg
clinical: In superior gluteal nerve injury the opposite side of the pelvis drops when the patient stands on one leg (positive Trendelenburg sign) and the gait waddles.
tus: Gluteus medius and minimus stop the pelvis dropping to the opposite side when standing on one leg.
Its anterior fibres internally rotate the hip.

m-gluteus-minimus.summary: The deepest and smallest of the gluteal muscles; it works together with gluteus medius.
facts: Outer surface of the ilium (between the anterior and inferior gluteal lines)
Anterior surface of the greater trochanter
Superior gluteal nerve (L4–S1)
Superior gluteal artery
Abducts and internally rotates the hip; stabilises the pelvis in walking
tus: Gluteus minimus lies beneath gluteus medius and is supplied by the same nerve (superior gluteal nerve).

m-tensor-fasciae-latae.summary: A muscle on the upper lateral thigh lying between two layers of fascia; it acts down to the knee through the iliotibial tract.
facts: Anterior superior iliac spine and anterior part of the iliac crest
Iliotibial tubercle of the tibia (Gerdy's tubercle) via the iliotibial tract
Superior gluteal nerve (L4–S1)
Lateral circumflex femoral artery, superior gluteal artery
Abducts, internally rotates and flexes the hip; stabilises the extended knee
tus: TFL stabilises the extended knee through the iliotibial tract.

tractus-iliotibialis.summary: A strong fibrous band on the lateral thigh formed by a thickening of the fascia lata. Gluteus maximus and tensor fasciae latae insert into it.
facts: From the iliac crest to the iliotibial tubercle of the tibia
Stabilises the extended knee and the hip laterally
clinical: In runners, friction of the band over the lateral femoral epicondyle causes pain on the outer knee (iliotibial band syndrome).
tus: Iliotibial band syndrome in runners presents with pain over the lateral femoral condyle.

mm-rotatores-coxae.summary: A deep group of muscles behind the hip joint that rotate the thigh outwards. Piriformis is the key muscle of the region.
facts: Piriformis: front of the sacrum; obturator internus: inner surface of the obturator membrane; gemelli: ischial spine (superior) and ischial tuberosity (inferior); quadratus femoris: ischial tuberosity; obturator externus: outer surface of the obturator membrane
Greater trochanter and trochanteric fossa; quadratus femoris: intertrochanteric crest

Piriformis: S1–S2; obturator internus and gemellus superior: nerve to obturator internus (L5–S2); quadratus femoris and gemellus inferior: nerve to quadratus femoris (L4–S1); obturator externus: obturator nerve
Superior and inferior gluteal arteries, internal pudendal artery, medial circumflex femoral artery
Rotate the thigh outwards and hold the head of the femur in the acetabulum; with the hip flexed piriformis abducts
sections: It divides the greater sciatic foramen: above it (suprapiriform) pass the superior gluteal nerve and vessels; below it (infrapiriform) the sciatic nerve, inferior gluteal nerve, pudendal nerve, posterior femoral cutaneous nerve and inferior gluteal vessels.
clinical: Piriformis syndrome: pain radiating from the buttock down the leg due to compression of the sciatic nerve by the muscle.
tus: The short lateral rotators: piriformis, gemellus superior and inferior, obturator internus and externus, quadratus femoris.
All except obturator externus are supplied by branches of the sacral plexus; obturator externus is supplied by the obturator nerve.

m-sartorius.summary: The longest muscle in the body, crossing obliquely from lateral to medial across the front of the thigh. It is named the 'tailor's muscle' because it produces the cross-legged sitting position.
facts: Anterior superior iliac spine
Upper medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus)
Femoral nerve (L2–L3)
Muscular branches of the femoral artery
Flexes, abducts and externally rotates the hip; flexes the knee
sections: The tendons of sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus join on the medial surface of the tibia in a goose-foot shape (pes anserinus). Memory aid: 'SGT – Say Grace before Tea'.
clinical: It forms the lateral border of the femoral triangle and the anterior boundary of the adductor (Hunter's) canal; it is an important landmark for reaching the femoral vessels.
tus: Sartorius is the lateral border of the femoral triangle and the roof of the adductor canal.

m-quadriceps-femoris.summary: The four-headed muscle forming most of the anterior compartment of the thigh: rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis and vastus intermedius. It is the only powerful extensor of the knee.
facts: Rectus femoris: anterior inferior iliac spine and upper rim of the acetabulum; vastus lateralis: greater trochanter and lateral lip of the linea aspera; vastus medialis: intertrochanteric line and medial lip of the linea aspera; vastus intermedius: anterolateral surface of the femoral shaft
Patella via the common quadriceps tendon, and the tibial tuberosity via the patellar ligament
Femoral nerve (L2–L4)
Lateral circumflex femoral artery, femoral artery, profunda femoris artery
Extends the knee; rectus femoris also flexes the hip (the only head crossing two joints)
clinical: The patellar reflex (L3–L4) is the stretch reflex of this muscle group.
In femoral nerve injury knee extension is lost and the patient cannot climb stairs.
Vastus medialis atrophies fastest after knee surgery or immobilisation.
tus: The patellar reflex assesses segments L3–L4 (especially L4).
Quadriceps tendon rupture is more common in older people, patellar tendon rupture in younger people.

mm-adductores.summary: The muscle group in the medial compartment of the thigh that draws the legs together. Adductor magnus is the largest of the group and has two parts.
facts: Body and inferior ramus of the pubis; hamstring part of adductor magnus: ischial tuberosity
Linea aspera of the femur; hamstring part of adductor magnus: adductor tubercle
Obturator nerve (L2–L4); hamstring part of adductor magnus: tibial part of the sciatic nerve (L4)
Profunda femoris artery, obturator artery
Adduct the thigh; assist flexion and rotation; stabilise the pelvis in walking
sections: Through the opening in adductor magnus (adductor hiatus) the femoral artery and vein pass behind the knee and become the popliteal artery and vein.
clinical: In athletes a groin strain most often affects adductor longus.
tus: The adductor group (longus, brevis, magnus, gracilis, pectineus) is supplied mainly by the obturator nerve.
Groin strain most often involves adductor longus.

m-gracilis.summary: The most superficial, long and slender muscle on the medial thigh; the only muscle of the medial compartment crossing both hip and knee.
facts: Body and inferior ramus of the pubis
Upper medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus)
Obturator nerve (L2–L3)
Profunda femoris artery, obturator artery
Adducts the thigh and flexes and internally rotates the knee
clinical: The muscle is often used in plastic surgery as a functional free muscle flap.
tus: Gracilis can be used as a muscle flap and its tendon as a graft (ACL reconstruction); it is supplied by the obturator nerve.

m-pectineus.summary: A quadrilateral muscle in the floor of the femoral triangle, between iliopsoas and adductor longus.
facts: Pecten pubis (pectineal line) of the pubis
Pectineal line of the femur (below the lesser trochanter)
Femoral nerve (L2–L3), sometimes also fibres from the obturator nerve
Medial circumflex femoral artery, obturator artery
Adducts and flexes the thigh
tus: Pectineus forms part of the floor of the femoral triangle.

mm-ischiocrurales.summary: Three muscles forming the posterior compartment of the thigh that extend the hip and flex the knee. Biceps femoris lies laterally, semitendinosus and semimembranosus medially.
facts: Ischial tuberosity (short head of biceps femoris: lateral lip of the linea aspera)
Biceps femoris: head of the fibula; semitendinosus: upper medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus); semimembranosus: posterior surface of the medial condyle of the tibia
Tibial part of the sciatic nerve (L5–S2); short head of biceps femoris: common fibular part
Perforating arteries (profunda femoris artery), medial circumflex femoral artery
Extend the hip and flex the knee; biceps femoris rotates the knee outwards, semitendinosus and semimembranosus inwards
clinical: Hamstring tears are among the most common muscle injuries in sprinters.
In anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction the semitendinosus (and gracilis) tendon is often used as a graft.
tus: The hamstrings extend the hip and flex the knee; avulsion from the ischial tuberosity occurs in athletes.
Hamstring tightness can limit the straight leg raise test; it should not be confused with sciatic nerve stretch signs.

m-biceps-femoris.summary: A two-headed hamstring muscle on the posterolateral thigh. Its tendon can be felt on the lateral side of the back of the knee.
facts: Long head: ischial tuberosity; short head: lateral lip of the linea aspera
Head of the fibula
Long head: tibial part; short head: common fibular part (L5–S2)
Perforating arteries, inferior gluteal artery
Flexes the knee and rotates the flexed knee outwards; the long head extends the hip
clinical: The common fibular nerve, running just medial and posterior to its tendon, can be injured in surgery on the lateral knee.
tus: Biceps femoris is a dynamic stabiliser of the lateral knee and inserts on the fibular head; the common fibular nerve runs just behind its tendon.
